source: Wu et al. (2023/2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Closest LLM analogue to Soloway's unplan-like programs. Models write and trace code well under the default convention but lose much of it when a familiar convention is changed (1-based indexing in a Python variant called ThonPy) while the task stays the same.
numbers: HumanEval code generation, subset of 53 tasks where 1-based execution changes the answer, pass@1 default to counterfactual: GPT-4 82.5 to 40.5, GPT-3.5 68.9 to 25.1, Claude 47.6 to 15.7, PaLM-2 29.2 to 7.4. Pass@10 GPT-4 93.3 to 64.9. Full 164 tasks, GPT-4 pass@1 87.4 to 68.2. Code execution (113 instances) GPT-4 58.4 to 18.6.
limits: Tests a changed language rule, not an odd but legal program. Models are 2023 era (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2). Not a Soloway fill-in-the-blank replication.
agent_relevance: Gives indirect support for gap 2: a strong model leans on the default convention and pays a large price when the task departs from it. Retrieved plan hints that encode the default will add to this pull. A direct plan-like versus unplan-like fill-in test on a current model is still unrun.

source: Dinh, Zhao, Tan, Negrinho, Lausen, Zha, Karypis (2023) Large Language Models of Code Fail at Completing Code with Potential Bugs (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: When the code context already contains a likely bug, code models keep following the context and complete badly. This is a measured case of context-induced expectation: the model continues the pattern it was shown.
numbers: buggy-HumanEval, CodeGen-2B-mono test-case pass rate 54.9% with the reference partial code against 3.1% with a partial code that has a potential bug. Pass rates fell below 5% across both datasets (buggy-HumanEval and buggy-FixEval) for all tested model variants. The same failure pattern (completion that matches the buggy context) is reported in about 90% of instances.
limits: Small 2023 code models, not current frontier models. One synthetic bug type (operator flips) plus real user bugs. Post-hoc fixes tested only partly closed the gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and gap 2. A wrong or mismatched item in context is followed, not questioned. A stored plan injected into the prompt needs a check step (run it, compare to the task) or it can be followed as the buggy prefix was.

source: Lam, Wang, Huang, Lyu (2025) CodeCrash: Exposing LLM Fragility to Misleading Natural Language in Code Reasoning
finding: Plausible but wrong natural-language hints (comments, messages, hints about expected output) pull models toward the hint instead of tracing the code. Reasoning models resist better but can spend far more tokens arguing with a wrong hint.
numbers: 1,279 questions from CRUXEval and LiveCodeBench, 17 LLMs. Average relative pass@1 drop 23.2% on output prediction; with chain-of-thought 13.8%. Large reasoning models (o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B) are more robust but a plausible wrong hint caused 2 to 3 times the reasoning tokens, and QwQ-32B showed a collapse in extreme cases. Increasing o3-mini effort made the drop worse.
quote: plausible yet incorrect hints can trigger pathological self-reflection
limits: Code reasoning (output and input prediction), not code writing. Hints are wrong comments, not wrong retrieved plans. Models from early 2025.
agent_relevance: Best direct number for gap 6 on harm from a wrong hint. A wrong stored plan can cost both accuracy and tokens. Keep plan text out of the prompt until it passes a check, and cap the effort spent on disputing it.

source: Wu, Li, Tafjord, Kim (2026) XYEval: Agents say yes to bad advice
finding: Current frontier agents lose a lot of task score when a user adds a plausible but misleading suggestion about how to solve the task. A general warning in the system prompt only partly helps. Naming the exact distractor (an unrealistic upper bound) helps much more.
numbers: Five models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT 5.5), six benchmark suites. Relative drops up to 46.7% (Terminal-Bench, Gemini 3.1 Pro 67.4 to 36.0). SWE-bench Verified original to misled: 77.2 to 68.8, 78.0 to 70.8, 79.8 to 71.4, 90.0 to 75.5 (Claude, -16.1%), 80.5 to 64.0. Models were more susceptible on easier benchmarks with higher baseline scores.
limits: The bad advice comes from a user turn, not from a retrieved library. Gemini 3.7 Flash on SWE-bench Pro rose 2.4%, so a wrong direction can also prompt useful exploration. Single reported run per cell in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 6, 2026 evidence on strong models: advice that looks like a plan is followed even by top models. Treat retrieved plans as hypotheses to test. A generic caution line is not enough.

source: Rivera, Steinmaurer, Fisler, Krishnamurthi (2024) Iterative Student Program Planning using Transformer-Driven Feedback (ITiCSE 2024)
finding: GPT-4 was used as a plan-to-code translator: a student's written plan is turned into code and run against tests, so the plan gets feedback. GPT-4 often repairs weak plans on its own, which is a risk to plan checking. GPT-3.5 and StarCoder gave too many false negatives.
numbers: 544 of 736 enrolled CS1 students submitted (Graz). Feedback on two functions: median 4 and 2 submissions (means 3.6, 2.6) against median 1 without feedback. 50 students hand-coded, kappa 0.8 to 1. Plans coded RIGHT-TRACK on first attempt: 39, of which 27 failed a majority of tests; on last attempt 42, of which 19 failed. False positives: only 13 INCORRECT or NO-ATTEMPT plans passed; 12 of 13 got 0/5 or 1/5 tests. One plan scored 4/5 once and 0/5 on a rerun. Cost over USD 200 for two feedback rounds. GPT-4 first gave many false positives because it filled in details; removing the problem statement from the prompt cut them.
limits: Experience report, one course, GPT-4-0613. Plans are student to-do lists, not stored library plans. Non-determinism of the LLM check is visible in the one outlier.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 6. A strong model executing a plan silently fills the plan's holes, so passing tests do not show the plan was sound. For our agent: judge a stored plan by running it with the problem statement withheld, and rerun to see the spread.

source: Crichton, Sampaio, Hanrahan (2021) Automating Program Structure Classification (SIGCSE 2021)
finding: Student Rainfall solutions can be assigned to Fisler's three plan-composition structures (Single Loop, Clean First, Clean Multiple) automatically. A nearest-neighbour rule using syntax-tree edit distance needs few examples; an RNN needs more. Errors are structured: Single Loop is almost always mistaken for Clean Multiple.
numbers: Up to 91% accuracy when trained on 108 programs, OCaml and Pyret data from Fisler's study. OCaml nearest-neighbour about 85% against RNN lower at small training size; Pyret nearest-neighbour 67% and RNN about 79% at a small training size (condition read from the text, partly unclear). RNN needed at least 100 examples in OCaml; nearest-neighbour much fewer. Fisler hand-coding took 1 to 2 minutes per program.
limits: One problem (Rainfall), two functional languages, human labels from one lab. Surface syntax similarity misleads where plans differ in where filtering happens. Pre-LLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. A structural key (tree edit distance) works with a handful of labeled examples but confuses plans that differ in one placement choice, which is exactly the composition choice. Combine with a role key or an LLM label.

source: Wang, Yang, et al. (2024) CodeRAG-Bench: Can Retrieval Augment Code Generation?
finding: Retrieval helps code generation, but mostly where the model lacks knowledge. Strong models gain little on common material, and extra context can hurt. Retrievers fail when the query and the useful document share few words. Dense retrievers often beat BM25.
numbers: Adding retrieved library documents on ODEX-hard (20 least-used libraries) improved results by 20.3 to 40.1 points depending on method. GPT-4o gained 27.4 with gold documents on SWE-bench Lite. DeepSeekCoder-7B did not improve on MBPP with retrieved context (over-long, repetitive outputs) while StarCoder2 gained 15.6 to 17.8 over the canonical setup. Jina-v2-code beat GIST-base by 7.4 average NDCG@10; BM25 index 141MB, 0.02 ms search against dense models up to 316 ms encoding.
limits: Retrieves documents, snippets and tutorials, not stereotyped plans. Models from 2024. Numbers read from text, not every table.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5 and 6. Supports a small, targeted library, not a large one. A retrieval key must bridge the gap between the task wording and the plan role words; use a description that restates the role, not only code text.

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2023/2024) LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code (ICLR 2024)
finding: A library of compressed abstractions with anonymous names did not help an LLM solver and in some cases hurt it. Adding an automatic name and docstring for each abstraction (AutoDoc) restored use. This is a direct test of the retrieval key and label question for reusable solved parts.
numbers: Relative to the LLM Solver baseline, anonymous Stitch abstractions changed solve rate by -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO). AutoDoc then added +9.73 (REGEX) and +2.27 (CLEVR) over the anonymous condition and +0.00 on LOGO, where semantic errors in the descriptions were the cause. Full LILO reached best mean test solve rates in the tables (for example REGEX 77.07 against LLM Solver 76.13, LOGO 48.95 against 32.13 on the first block of the table).
limits: Domain-specific languages (string editing, scene reasoning, graphics), Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 era models, 3 seeded runs, wide standard deviations. Table columns are partly garbled in the text so only the quoted text deltas are relied on.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6. Stored solved parts without role names and one-line meaning can lower accuracy; a wrong description (the LOGO case) removes the gain. Store a name, a role sentence and a test with every plan.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (ICLR 2025), harm and quality section
finding: The AWM authors state that offline workflows induced from training examples are not always correct and can lead to incorrect workflows that degrade performance. The numbers are mixed rather than a clean harm rate.
numbers: Mind2Web, MindAct baseline against AWM-offline: cross-task step success 36.2 to 45.1 but action F1 60.6 to 57.3; cross-website step success 30.1 to 33.7 but action F1 51.1 to 46.2; cross-domain step success 18.6 to 32.6 and action F1 52.8 to 41.6. Online AWM generalized better to unseen sites. Induced workflows: 7.3 to 7.4 per example, utility rate 0.91 (Mind2Web) and 0.94 (WebArena), coverage 0.40, function overlap 0.08 to 0.20.
limits: Web navigation, not code. No measured rate of wrong stored workflows, nor harm split by verification strength. Some trends are read from a partly garbled table.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open for code. Hint that memory built from unverified training runs trades one metric (step success) against another (action F1). Build the library only from verified solutions and log use versus no-use.

source: Ma, He, Snell, Griggs, Min, Zaharia (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: At equal token budget, skipping the long thinking block (NoThinking) with many parallel samples matches or beats thinking, especially at low budget and high k. Coding is the exception at pass@1.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. Under about 3,000 tokens NoThinking beat Thinking at every k; around 3,500 tokens Thinking led at pass@1 and NoThinking passed it from k=2. Example: ACM 23 with 700 tokens, 51.3 against 28.9. On LiveCodeBench, Thinking stayed ahead at pass@1 even at low budget because disabling the box barely cut tokens. Parallel NoThinking with a verifier or best-of-N matched Thinking with up to 9 times longer latency.
limits: Distilled open model, budget forcing, math-heavy suite plus one coding set. Does not test an explicit plan stage.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. At equal tokens many cheap samples with a check beat one long thought, except for code pass@1. Spending tokens on an explicit plan stage must beat this baseline, not only direct generation.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
finding: On SWE-bench Verified, reasoning models plan and reflect more than non-reasoning ones, with higher overthinking scores, and more reasoning effort does not buy more fixes. Choosing the lowest-overthinking of several runs improved results and cut cost.
numbers: Reasoning models showed overthinking scores nearly three times higher than non-reasoning models. o1 with high effort resolved 29.1% at USD 1,400; low effort resolved 27.3% at 43% lower cost; selecting the lowest overthinking-score run of two gave 30.3% with 15% less compute than the high setting.
limits: Agentic issue resolution, not isolated code writing. Early 2025 models (o1, DeepSeek). Page text read in part (abstract, introduction and figures).
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Models that already plan inside their thinking do not gain from extra visible planning cost. Count tokens, prefer a cheap second sample with a check over a longer plan.

source: Think Anywhere in Code Generation (2026 preprint, authors not captured in the extracted text)
finding: Planning only up front is insufficient for code: problems show up during implementation. Letting the model think at points inside the code beat up-front thinking, with fewer tokens. A model trained this way keeps most of its gain even without any up-front thinking.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B based, pass@1 average over LeetCode, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval, MBPP: base 61.0, Think-Anywhere 70.3 (+9.3). Ablation: no up-front thinking 66.6 (-2.8 against 69.4), line-level thinking 67.2, padding tokens 67.6, RL only 63.4, cold start only 47.9. Token cost lower than GRPO (up-front) and CoT in every benchmark of the token figure. Self-planning and interleaved thinking were baselines; their exact rows could not be parsed from the extracted table.
limits: Needs training (cold start plus RL) on a 7B model, so not a scaffold result. Authors are the proposers. The prompting variant was weaker than the trained one. The table text was scrambled for baseline rows.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. A plan chosen before coding does not cover issues that appear while writing. A scaffold should allow a re-plan or a check point inside implementation, not only a plan state before it.

source: Denny, Prather, Becker, et al. (2023/2024) Computing Education in the Era of Generative AI (CACM), section on Codex and the Rainfall problem
finding: The only LLM study found that touches Rainfall: Codex was run on seven Rainfall problem wordings. It reports correctness and variety of solution structure, not plan-composition errors. Codex scored well on CS1 exams but poorly on edge cases.
numbers: Rainfall: 7 variants, 50 responses each, 350 programs, 10 tests each (3,500 evaluations); average score close to 50%; poor when no valid values were given (empty collection). Exams: 15.7/20 (78.5%) and 19.5/25 (78.0%), ranked 17th of 71 students.
limits: Survey article reporting an earlier Codex study; Codex is outdated. No plan-composition coding of the programs, no per-structure bug shares.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 narrows only slightly: LLMs fail Rainfall on guard cases (empty input), the same missing-guard slot humans miss. A current-model Rainfall run with Fisler's three-structure coding is still undone.

source: Fisler and Castro (2017) Sometimes, Rainfall Accumulates: Talk-Alouds with Novice Functional Programmers (ICER 2017)
finding: Students who have seen several valid schemas for Rainfall pick one by familiarity and are stuck by the pattern they know best. The authors say teaching a general approach (an accumulator) with only single-use examples leaves students unable to adapt it. They do not report that de Raadt's strategy teaching changed plan choice.
numbers: 13 students talked aloud for 30 minutes in Racket in week 7 of an 8-week CS1; four narratives reported. Students had seen only structural traversals and single-accumulator functions. Authors note de Raadt et al. used Rainfall to test teaching of planning strategies but do not discuss strategy change.
limits: Qualitative, 4 narratives of 13, one course. No effect sizes. Does not provide the de Raadt numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (partial). Fixation on a known pattern is a human analogue to a retrieved plan taking over. A library should store several plan variants per goal and make the agent choose between them against the task constraints.

source: Soloway and Ehrlich (1984) Empirical studies of programming knowledge, IEEE TSE SE-10(5); Spohrer, Soloway, Pope (1985); Gilmore and Green (1988); Pennington (1987)
finding: Search for gap 7 and gap 10: no full text could be reached this session. The queensu soloway84.pdf link returned a different Soloway 1984 paper (a short methodology note on designing languages, not the TSE study). Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors and the web search budget ran out before Spohrer 1985, Gilmore and Green 1988 or Pennington 1987 could be searched. A web search snippet repeated the known summary only.
numbers: No new figures. The 75% PROUST figure remains unverified; Gilmore and Green and Pennington numbers remain second-hand via Detienne 1990 (a12, a13).
limits: Negative result, not a finding about the papers. Do not cite as evidence for or against.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 10 stay open. Keep K01 at single-source and K20 at contested.

source: Fisler (2014) An empirical study of student plan composition in functional programming (download attempt)
finding: The retry to open the 2014 paper by guessed Brown URL returned a 179-byte HTML error page, not the PDF. The 3 of 187 composition errors and 5% no-plan figures stay second-hand (b06, b08).
numbers: None new. Crichton 2021 (d06) confirms from the dataset side that Fisler's three structures (Single Loop, Clean First, Clean Multiple) cover a large majority of solutions.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and K06 cannot be re-checked here; use d06 only as a side confirmation of the structure categories.
